briefs.learning_objective: Learner can define the problem statement and boundary of a BA effort before eliciting solution requirements.

required_facts.statement: Problem framing clarifies the problem rather than choosing a solution.
Write a concise problem statement identifying who is affected, what the problem is, why it matters, and where it occurs.
State what work is included and what is excluded to make the scope boundary explicit.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can plan and run a structured one-on-one stakeholder interview using a fixed question set to elicit requirements.

required_facts.statement: A structured interview follows an interview script, unlike a semistructured interview’s flexibly ordered guide.
source_refs: nngroup_articles#https://www.nngroup.com/articles/interview-guide/ — Opening definitions of interview script and interview guide

required_facts.statement: Define what needs to be learned and prepare questions that address those aims.
source_refs: nngroup_articles#https://www.nngroup.com/articles/interview-guide/ — Step 1: Write Your Research Questions; Step 4: Fill In for Unaccounted Research Questions

required_facts.statement: Ask concise, open-ended questions that let the participant describe their experience without suggesting the answer.
Record the elicited needs in a shared requirements document with links to the supporting interview context.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Step 4: Document requirements in one shared place

required_facts.statement: Probe vague answers with follow-up questions about concrete expected outcomes, operating conditions and constraints, and observable or measurable criteria showing that the requirement has been met.
source_refs: nngroup_articles#https://www.nngroup.com/articles/interview-guide/ — Step 6: Prepare Additional Probing and Followup Questions

atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Step 1: Define the project goal; Step 3: Collect input through the right channels; What to include in a requirements document — Assumptions, Constraints, Acceptance criteria

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can plan and run a facilitated group workshop (e.g. a JAD session) to elicit requirements from multiple stakeholders at once.

required_facts.statement: A workshop uses goal-oriented group activities and discussion to produce shared outcomes.
Build the agenda by defining goals, identifying questions needed to reach them, and choosing activities that answer those questions.
Allocate time to each workshop segment and prepare the materials needed to capture discussion.
Guide discussion toward the agenda goals and analyze and share the collected outputs after the workshop.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can design a survey/questionnaire to elicit requirements or preferences from a large or dispersed stakeholder population.

required_facts.statement: Surveys are best suited to collecting quantitative attitudinal data rather than detailed accounts of behavior.
source_refs: nngroup_articles#https://www.nngroup.com/articles/survey-best-practices/ — Don’t Ask Questions that Respondents Can’t Answer Accurately

required_facts.statement: Include questions needed to answer the research aims rather than collecting information simply because it is easy to ask for.
source_refs: nngroup_articles#https://www.nngroup.com/articles/survey-best-practices/ — Don’t Ask Questions that You Can Find the Answer to

required_facts.statement: Write questions that respondents can answer accurately and avoid language that leads them toward a preferred answer.
source_refs: nngroup_articles#https://www.nngroup.com/articles/survey-best-practices/ — Don’t Ask Questions that Respondents Can’t Answer Accurately; Avoid Biasing Respondents

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can extract requirements and constraints by systematically reviewing existing artifacts (contracts, manuals, prior specs).

required_facts.statement: Existing documentation is one channel for gathering requirements.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Step 3: Collect input through the right channels

required_facts.statement: Extract the requirements, assumptions, constraints, and open questions found in existing material and record them in one shared document with links to supporting context.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Step 3: Collect input through the right channels; Step 4: Document requirements in one shared place

required_facts.statement: Confirm the documented requirements with stakeholders before treating them as execution work.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can elicit requirements by watching users perform their actual work (job shadowing) rather than asking them to describe it.

required_facts.statement: Observation examines what users do in their work context rather than relying solely on their account of what they do.
Watch the user perform work, then ask questions about what was observed.
Record the tasks performed and analyze their sequence and subtasks to understand how the goal is achieved.
Record the user’s stated process, compare it with the steps observed during actual work, and log discrepancies with notes of the observed actions that support them.
source_refs: nngroup_articles#https://www.nngroup.com/articles/contextual-inquiry/ — When to Use Contextual Inquiry; The 4 Phases of Contextual Inquiry — 1. The primer, 3. The contextual interview, 4. The wrapup

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can verify that a set of requirements is complete, unambiguous, and testable, and validate that it matches the actual business need.

required_facts.statement: Validation with stakeholders confirms priorities and agreement about what will be delivered.
For the requirements review, present the documented goal, scope, requirements, assumptions, and open questions, then capture stakeholder agreement or requested changes.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Step 4: Document requirements in one shared place; Step 5: Prioritize and validate requirements

required_facts.statement: Distinguish validation of the intended business need with stakeholders from verification of the written requirements’ quality: stakeholder agreement does not by itself establish that the wording is unambiguous or objectively testable.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/acceptance-criteria — Characteristics of good acceptance criteria — Clarity and conciseness; Testability

required_facts.statement: Check completeness against the documented goals, success metrics, scope, requirement categories, assumptions, and constraints; record missing information as open questions for resolution.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Step 4: Document requirements in one shared place

required_facts.statement: Check ambiguity by asking whether stakeholders can interpret the statement the same way; replace vague wording with plain, outcome-focused language and measurable thresholds where possible.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/acceptance-criteria — Characteristics of good acceptance criteria — Clarity and conciseness; Measurability

required_facts.statement: Check testability by identifying an executable test and an objective pass/fail result for each stated condition; revise a condition if its satisfaction depends on subjective judgment.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/acceptance-criteria — Characteristics of good acceptance criteria — Testability; How to write acceptance criteria — 3. Establish overall testability

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can use low-fidelity prototypes/wireframes as an elicitation tool to surface requirements stakeholders can't articulate verbally.

required_facts.statement: A low-fidelity prototype is an inexpensive, relatively simple representation used to explore and test a design.
Sketch a wireframe by drawing the screen’s main content areas and controls without detailed visual styling.
Use a prototype to gather feedback about a design before investing in a fully implemented version.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can facilitate a divergent-thinking brainstorming session to generate a wide candidate set of ideas or requirements before narrowing.

required_facts.statement: Brainstorming generates alternative ideas for a shared problem.
State the session’s problem and goal, set a time limit, choose a facilitator, and record contributed ideas.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-collaboration/brainstorming/how-to-run-a-brainstorming-session — Step 1. Identify your goal; Step 3. Set a time and place; Step 4. Pick a qualified facilitator

required_facts.statement: Keep idea generation separate from judging ideas so participants can explore possibilities.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can run a moderated focus group discussion to elicit requirements or reactions from a representative stakeholder sample.

required_facts.statement: A focus group is a moderated discussion that gathers participants’ attitudes and opinions.
Prepare a moderator script with specific issues and goals for the information to be gathered.
Keep discussion on topic, invite all participants to contribute, and prevent one participant from dominating.
Record the opinions and disagreements expressed in the discussion without treating those stated preferences as evidence of actual product use.
source_refs: nngroup_articles#https://www.nngroup.com/articles/focus-groups/ — Getting Focused; opening distinction between what users say and do

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can identify risks embedded in a set of requirements that could threaten project or requirement success.

required_facts.statement: Gather information about known risks, blockers, and dependencies while eliciting requirements.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Step 3: Collect input through the right channels

required_facts.statement: A risk matrix evaluates a risk using its likelihood and impact.
Assess likelihood and impact for each identified risk and use its matrix position to determine a risk level.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/risk-matrix — How to create a risk matrix

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can author a Business Requirements Document (BRD) that captures business need, objectives, and high-level requirements for sign-off.

required_facts.statement: Business requirements express the broader business goal or outcome the work should support.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Types of project requirements to gather

required_facts.statement: A requirements document can contain a project summary, goals and success metrics, in-scope and out-of-scope items, requirements, assumptions, and constraints.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Step 4: Document requirements in one shared place

required_facts.statement: Organize the elicited requirements in that shared structure and review them with approvers to agree what will be delivered.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can author a Functional Specification that translates business requirements into detailed system behavior.

required_facts.statement: Functional requirements state what the deliverable must do.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Types of project requirements to gather

required_facts.statement: Document the expected functions separately from the broader business outcome and from how the solution should perform.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Types of project requirements to gather; Step 4

required_facts.statement: Write a detailed functional specification entry with the initiating event and input values, the expected system response, resulting outputs, and applicable preconditions, postconditions, or exception behavior.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can write a user story in standard format with Given-When-Then acceptance criteria that make it independently testable.

required_facts.statement: A user story describes a desired outcome from a user’s perspective.
Write a story as “As a [persona], I [want to], [so that].” to state the user, need, and purpose.
Acceptance criteria describe specific conditions that must be satisfied for the story to be accepted.
Write each acceptance scenario on separate lines using “Given …”, “When …”, and “Then …” in that order.
source_refs: https://cucumber.io/docs/gherkin/reference/#Example — scenario pattern; Steps; Given; When; Then

required_facts.statement: Given sets the initial context or precondition, When describes the action or event, and Then states an expected result observable to the user or an external system.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can write a use case specification describing actor goals, main flow, and alternate flows for a system interaction.

required_facts.statement: A use case specifies behavior that provides an observable result of value to an actor or other stakeholder.
An actor represents a role interacting with the subject and may be a person or another system.
Describe a use case’s behavior in natural language with relevant preconditions and postconditions.
Include the basic interaction and relevant variations, exceptional behavior, or error handling.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can build and maintain a requirements traceability matrix linking requirements to their source, design, and test artifacts.

required_facts.statement: Requirements traceability maintains links from initial business needs through design, development, and testing to the work that fulfills the requirements.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/jira/templates/requirements-traceability-matrix — What is a requirements traceability matrix template?

required_facts.statement: Construct an RTM with a row for each requirement identifier and columns for its originating business need or source, related design artifact, and test-case identifiers; populate these with references to the actual artifacts rather than unlinked descriptions.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/jira/templates/requirements-traceability-matrix — What is a requirements traceability matrix template?; How to get started — 2. Define and categorize requirements for easy traceability; 3. Link requirements to related work items

required_facts.statement: When a requirement changes, follow its links to identify affected work items that need updating.

Review the RTM for missing required links: a requirement without a source link is orphaned from its business justification, and a missing design or test link is a coverage gap when that artifact is required for the stage being reviewed.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/jira/templates/requirements-traceability-matrix — What is a requirements traceability matrix template?; Importance of a requirements traceability matrix template; How to get started — 3. Link requirements to related work items; 5. Track progress with dashboards and reports

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can manage a requirement's lifecycle from draft through approval, change, and retirement, tracking version and status.

required_facts.statement: Requirements documentation needs updating as development and learning change the understanding of the work.
Track the current program status and keep requirements linked to current work-item status.
For a changed requirement, identify and update related work through its traceability links.

Use a customized requirement workflow to distinguish draft (under preparation or review), approved (agreed for delivery), change under review (a proposed revision awaiting a decision), and retired (no longer current); make approval, revision review, and retirement explicit status transitions rather than silently overwriting the current requirement.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/jira/templates/document-approval — Workflows; Easy document management; Progress tracking; Customized workflow
atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/itsm/change-management — Change management process — Change request; Change request review; Change approval; Change closure

required_facts.statement: For a proposed change, record the affected requirement and change request, review its risks and expected outcomes, record the approval decision and status, then document the implemented change and its results.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/itsm/change-management — Change management process — Change request; Change request review; Change plan; Change approval; Change implementation; Change closure

required_facts.statement: When the requirement is documented on a Confluence page, modifying that page creates a new version; record the current workflow status in the document, and use More options > Page History to inspect version numbers and compare the revision with the preceding version.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://confluence.atlassian.com/doc/page-history-and-page-comparison-views-139379.html — Access the page history; View the changes made; Compare two versions

optional_enrichment.statement: Preserve the change history when restoring an earlier requirement document: Confluence restoration creates a new current copy of the selected version rather than replacing the historical versions, and lets the user edit the restoration’s change comment.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can identify and write non-functional requirements (performance, security, usability, reliability) distinct from functional behavior.

required_facts.statement: Nonfunctional requirements describe how the solution should perform or operate rather than the functions it must provide.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Types of project requirements to gather

required_facts.statement: Make the performance expectation measurable by stating a concrete numerical target rather than a vague request for good performance.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Types of project requirements to gather — non-functional requirements

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can identify all stakeholders for an initiative and classify them by role, interest, and authority.

required_facts.statement: A stakeholder is someone interested in the work or someone whose involvement is needed to complete it.
Identify people who use, provide input to, approve, fund, or are affected by the deliverable.
Classify stakeholders as directly involved or affected, indirectly affected or consulted, and reviewers or approvers, noting that roles can overlap.
Record each stakeholder’s role and assess their interest and power over the work.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can place stakeholders on an influence-interest (power-interest) grid to determine engagement strategy per quadrant.

required_facts.statement: Plot stakeholders on a grid with separate low-to-high power and interest axes.
Manage high-power, high-interest stakeholders closely.
Keep high-power, low-interest stakeholders satisfied.
Keep low-power, high-interest stakeholders informed.
Monitor low-power, low-interest stakeholders with less intensive engagement.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can build a RACI matrix assigning Responsible/Accountable/Consulted/Informed roles across tasks and stakeholders.

required_facts.statement: A RACI chart assigns roles by task to clarify who does work and who owns the outcome.
Responsible identifies the person or people doing the work.
Accountable identifies the one person ultimately answerable for a task’s completion.
Consulted identifies people whose input is needed, using two-way communication.
Informed identifies people kept updated, using one-way communication.
List tasks against stakeholders and assign the appropriate R, A, C, or I entries, checking that each task has one accountable owner.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/raci-chart — How to create a RACI chart

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can create a stakeholder engagement plan defining communication frequency, channel, and approach per stakeholder group.

required_facts.statement: A communication plan turns stakeholder analysis into specific ongoing engagement actions.
For each stakeholder group, specify the communication goal, channel, frequency, and owner.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook/plays/stakeholder-communications-plan — 3. Fill out the Communications Plan; 4. Review the Communications Plan

required_facts.statement: Match communication intensity to stakeholder power and interest and review whether the approach is effective.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can apply facilitation techniques (agenda control, time-boxing, managing dominant voices) to run any effective meeting or workshop.

required_facts.statement: A workshop facilitator supports the group’s process by planning, guiding, and managing collaborative work.
Use an agenda whose activities and allotted time support the meeting’s goals.
Redirect dominating contributions toward shared goals or invite other participants to balance the discussion.
source_refs: nngroup_articles#https://www.nngroup.com/articles/dominating-workshop-participants/ — How to Navigate Dominating Behaviors in a Workshop

required_facts.statement: Use silent individual contributions when verbal discussion prevents equitable participation.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can apply consensus-building and conflict-resolution techniques when stakeholders disagree on requirements or priorities.

required_facts.statement: Different stakeholders may have conflicting goals and different measures of success.
Build shared understanding by involving stakeholders in discussion of goals and evidence rather than presenting an isolated solution.
Forced ranking or dot voting can help a group move toward consensus.
source_refs: nngroup_articles#https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ux-workshop-agendas/ — Step 3: Pick processes that will answer the questions

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can read and draw BPMN 2.0 core notation elements (events, tasks, gateways, sequence/message flows) correctly.

required_facts.statement: An event is something that happens during a process and is drawn as a circle.
A task is an atomic activity and is drawn as a rounded rectangle.
A gateway controls branching and convergence of sequence flows and is drawn as a diamond.
Sequence flow is a solid line with a solid arrowhead indicating the order of activities within a process.
Message flow is a dashed line with an open arrowhead and open circle showing messages between separate participants.
Draw activities and appropriate events or gateways, connecting execution order with sequence flows and communication between participants with message flows.

Select a thin single-circle start event to show where a process starts, a thin double-circle intermediate event for something occurring between its start and end, and a thick single-circle end event to show where a process path ends.
source_refs: bpmn_spec#https://www.omg.org/spec/BPMN/2.0.2/PDF — 10.5 — Events; 10.5.2 — Start Event; 10.5.3 — End Event; 10.5.4 — Intermediate Event

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can model an existing (as-is) business process in BPMN to document current-state behavior.

required_facts.statement: An as-is process map records the current process rather than a proposed redesign.
Identify the process’s start and end, collect information about its steps and decisions, and determine their sequence.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/process-mapping — How to create a process map

required_facts.statement: Represent the observed activities and routing with BPMN tasks, events, gateways, and sequence flows.
Review the map with those who perform the process to refine its accuracy.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/process-mapping — How to create a process map

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can model a proposed (to-be) business process in BPMN reflecting a redesigned future state.

required_facts.statement: A future-state process map shows how the process is intended to work after improvement.
Use the current-state map to identify improvements and draw a revised map reflecting the proposed changes.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/process-mapping — Benefits of process mapping; How to create a process map

required_facts.statement: Use BPMN tasks, events, gateways, and sequence flows to represent the revised activities and routing.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can identify gaps and bottlenecks by comparing as-is and to-be process models or examining process flow.

required_facts.statement: Process mapping can expose bottlenecks, redundant efforts, and unnecessary steps.
Inspect the mapped steps and handoffs for obstacles that impede efficient flow.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/process-mapping — How to create a process map

required_facts.statement: Compare current-state and future-state maps to identify specific differences and potential efficiency gains.
List the specific steps or handoffs where the map shows delay, redundancy, or missing work, and review these findings with process stakeholders.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/process-mapping — Benefits of process mapping; 6. Review and validate

required_facts.statement: Identify a bottleneck as a capacity-limited step that cannot keep pace, causing work to accumulate and limiting the whole workflow’s throughput, and cite the observed capacity, throughput, or accumulating-work evidence in the diagram annotation.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/bottlenecks — What is a bottleneck?; 5 strategies to rectify bottlenecks in your workflows and fix them for good — opening identification guidance

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can apply process improvement techniques (e.g. Lean waste elimination) to redesign a process for efficiency.

required_facts.statement: Lean process improvement aims to eliminate waste and improve value delivered by a process.
Inspect a process for non-value-adding steps and propose a change that removes or reduces the identified waste.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/lean-process-improvement — How to apply Lean process improvement within projects — 1. Determine potential areas for improvement; 2. Identify potential solutions

required_facts.statement: Agree an improvement action with the team, implement it, and review its effects to continue improving the process.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/lean-process-improvement — How to apply Lean process improvement within projects

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can identify and document business rules (constraints/policies) that govern process or system behavior.

required_facts.statement: Requirements documentation includes assumptions and constraints that govern the work.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Step 4: Document requirements in one shared place

required_facts.statement: Capture required approvals and operating constraints explicitly when documenting what the deliverable must do.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Types of project requirements to gather; Step 4

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can build a decision table that maps combinations of condition values to the correct action/outcome.

required_facts.statement: A decision table records how combinations of conditions produce outcomes, including complex logic such as business rules.
To construct a decision table, put the conditions and resulting actions in rows and give each decision rule a column containing a unique condition combination and its associated actions.

For a limited-entry decision table, mark a condition T when satisfied, F when not satisfied, and – when irrelevant to the outcome; mark an action X when it should occur and leave it blank when it should not occur.

Check completeness by listing all condition combinations and confirming each feasible combination has a rule column with its resulting action; a feasible combination without a rule is a gap, while infeasible combinations can be removed.

Check consistency by comparing the outcomes assigned to the same feasible condition combination across the written rules and table; incompatible outcomes for that combination expose a contradiction that needs resolution.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can build a decision tree that represents sequential branching logic for a decision with ordered conditions.

required_facts.statement: A decision tree represents choices and possible outcomes with branches.
Start with the initial decision, add branches for the possible answers, and continue with subsequent decisions and their outcomes.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/decision-tree — How to create a decision tree

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can identify the entities and their attributes relevant to a business domain from a narrative description.

required_facts.statement: An entity is a business thing being described; its attributes are descriptive properties of that thing.
Identify the business things that need describing and list the descriptive attributes needed for each.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can identify the column(s) that uniquely identify each row of a table.

required_facts.statement: A primary key constraint indicates that a column, or group of columns, can be used as a unique identifier for the rows of a table; this requires the values to be both unique and not null.
A table can have at most one primary key, and a primary key can span more than one column (a composite key, composed of two or more attributes).
Entity integrity requires that every table have a primary key, and that neither the primary key nor any part of it contain null values.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can use a foreign key to reference another table's primary key and maintain referential integrity.

required_facts.statement: A foreign key constraint specifies that the values in a column (or group of columns) of one table must match values appearing in some row of another, referenced table.
A null foreign key value also satisfies referential integrity; a non-null one must match an existing primary key value in the referenced table.
A row whose foreign key value is not found in the referenced table is called an orphan record; referential integrity is what prevents these.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can recognize and model a one-to-many relationship between two entities.

required_facts.statement: In a one-to-many (1:M) relationship, one row on the 'one' side relates to many rows on the 'many' side; for example, one department has many employees.

In the Customer/Order example, a customer can place a minimum of zero and a maximum of many orders, while an order relates to a maximum of one customer, so Order is the 'many' side (the many side is optional, since a customer doesn't need to place an order to be a customer); the foreign key CustID is placed in the Order table and must match a valid CustID in the Customer table.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can recognize a many-to-many relationship and resolve it with a junction/bridge table.

required_facts.statement: A many-to-many (M:N) relationship cannot be implemented directly in the relational model; it is resolved into two one-to-many relationships using a composite entity, also called a junction or bridge table.
The junction table must contain at least the primary keys of the two original tables, used as foreign keys, and may also contain additional attributes of its own.
The combination of the two original tables' primary keys, brought in as foreign keys, will make the primary key of the junction table (or, together with another attribute, can form it).
source_refs: database_design_open_textbook#ch8-Example of mapping an M:N binary relationship type

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can determine and notate the cardinality (one-to-many, many-to-many) of a relationship between two entities using crow's-foot notation.

required_facts.statement: Relationship cardinality expresses how many instances on either side can be related.
A one-to-many relationship has a column with unique values on one side and potentially repeated matching values on the other.
A many-to-many relationship permits repeated matching values on both sides.
Determine the relationship by checking whether each side permits one or multiple matching instances.
In crow’s-foot notation, a circle (ring) represents zero, a bar (dash) represents one, and a crow’s-foot represents many.
Pair a circle and bar for optional zero-or-one, two bars for mandatory exactly-one, a circle and crow’s-foot for optional zero-or-many, or a bar and crow’s-foot for mandatory one-or-many.
At each relationship end, place the minimum symbol inward and the maximum symbol closest to the entity box.
Draw a relationship line between the entities and annotate both ends with the symbol pair for the number of instances of that end’s entity that can relate to an instance of the other entity.

optional_enrichment.statement: Write UML multiplicity as lower..upper: the lower bound is the minimum allowed number of related instances, the upper bound is the maximum, and * denotes an unlimited upper bound.
Interpret 0..1 as optional with at most one related instance, 1 (equivalently 1..1) as exactly one, 0..* as zero or more, and 1..* as one or more.

For a binary relationship, translate the business statement about how many instances of one entity can relate to a fixed instance of the other into lower and upper bounds, and place those bounds at the end whose instances are being counted; repeat from the opposite direction to annotate both ends.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can draw an entity-relationship diagram representing entities, attributes, and relationships for a business domain.

required_facts.statement: A model diagram can show entity types, their attributes, and relationships between instances.

Draw named entity boxes with relevant attributes, clearly identify primary-key and foreign-key attributes, and connect related entities through each foreign key and its referenced key, marking the permitted multiplicities.
Use multiplicity labels such as 1, 0..1, 0..*, or 1..* to state the permitted numbers of related instances.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can distinguish a conceptual data model (business language, no implementation detail) from a logical data model (typed, normalized, implementation-ready).

required_facts.statement: A conceptual data model is a high-level business view of the domain, describing important entity classes, their characteristics and constraints, and their relationships rather than a technical database implementation.
source_refs: https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/data-modeling#Types of data models — Conceptual data models

required_facts.statement: A logical data model is a less abstract, implementation-independent view that details entities and relationships and their attributes, including attribute data types and lengths.
source_refs: https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/data-modeling#Types of data models — Logical data models

required_facts.statement: Logical models can specify identifying keys: Oracle Data Modeler allows a primary unique identifier composed of attributes to identify an entity occurrence and foreign unique identifiers that refer to identifiers in another entity.

Classify a high-level business-domain overview as conceptual and a more detailed structure with typed attributes, identifiers, and specified relationships as logical, using its level of detail and implementation independence as evidence.
source_refs: https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/data-modeling#Types of data models — Conceptual data models; Logical data models

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can map a stakeholder's business information needs to the data entities/attributes that would satisfy them.

required_facts.statement: Business entities and their descriptive attributes give a model the information used to describe a business domain.
Identify the reporting or filtering information needed and match each item to the entity attributes that can supply it.
source_refs: powerbi_docs#https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-bi/guidance/star-schema — Understand star schema; Star schema relevance to Power BI semantic models

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can understand that relational data is organized into tables of rows and columns, each table modeling one entity type.

required_facts.statement: A relation, also called a table, holds data where each row (also called a record or tuple) represents one group of related data values.
The columns of a table are also called fields or attributes.
A table has a name distinct from every other table in the database, contains no duplicate rows, and the sequence of its rows and columns is insignificant.
A database is composed of multiple tables, each holding data.
Each table should contain information about one kind of thing only, such as the Branch or the Customer, rather than mixing unrelated things in one table.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can write a SQL SELECT statement to retrieve specific columns and rows from a table.

required_facts.statement: SELECT retrieves data from a table; the select list names the desired output columns.
Write SELECT column1, column2, column3 FROM table_name; to retrieve the named columns.
SELECT * FROM table_name; retrieves all columns.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can combine matching rows from two tables on a shared key using INNER JOIN.

required_facts.statement: For each row of T1, an INNER JOIN produces a joined row for each row of T2 that satisfies the join condition; rows from either table with no match are dropped.
The join condition is written in an ON clause, a boolean expression of the same kind used in a WHERE clause, or as a USING clause when both tables use the same column name.
INNER is the default kind of join; writing JOIN alone (without CROSS, LEFT, RIGHT, or FULL) means an INNER JOIN.

optional_enrichment.statement: Joins of all types can be chained together, or nested, so a query can INNER JOIN across more than two tables.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can aggregate rows into summary groups using GROUP BY with aggregate functions (SUM, COUNT, AVG).

required_facts.statement: GROUP BY creates one result group for rows with the same grouping-column values.
source_refs: postgres_docs#https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/queries-table-expressions.html — 7.2.3 — The GROUP BY and HAVING Clauses

required_facts.statement: SUM computes a total.
Write SELECT group_column, SUM(value_column) FROM table_name GROUP BY group_column; for one total per group.
source_refs: postgres_docs#https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/queries-table-expressions.html — 7.2.3 — The GROUP BY and HAVING Clauses

required_facts.statement: In the ordinary grouping pattern, list each selected column outside aggregate functions in GROUP BY.
source_refs: postgres_docs#https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/queries-table-expressions.html — 7.2.3 — The GROUP BY and HAVING Clauses

optional_enrichment.statement: COUNT(*) counts rows, and AVG computes an arithmetic mean.
Selected columns outside aggregate functions must be grouped unless they are functionally dependent on the grouping columns.
source_refs: postgres_docs#https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/queries-table-expressions.html — 7.2.3 — The GROUP BY and HAVING Clauses

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can filter rows before aggregation with WHERE and filter grouped results after aggregation with HAVING.

required_facts.statement: WHERE selects input rows before grouping and aggregate calculation.
HAVING selects groups after grouping and aggregate calculation.
Use SELECT group_column, SUM(value_column) FROM table_name WHERE row_condition GROUP BY group_column HAVING SUM(value_column) > threshold; to apply both kinds of filtering.
source_refs: postgres_docs#https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/queries-table-expressions.html — 7.2.3 — The GROUP BY and HAVING Clauses

required_facts.statement: In comparisons, = means equal, <> means not equal, and < or > means less or greater than.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can choose appropriate SQL data types for columns and handle NULL (unknown/missing) values correctly in queries.

required_facts.statement: SQL column types distinguish integers, exact numeric values, text, dates, and Boolean values, among other types.
Choose a column type whose value category and range fit the information being stored.
NULL represents an unknown value, and ordinary comparisons with NULL yield unknown rather than true or false.
Use WHERE column_name IS NULL or WHERE column_name IS NOT NULL to test for missing values rather than = NULL.
COALESCE(value, replacement) returns the first non-NULL argument; use it in the SELECT list to substitute for a missing value.
WHERE retains only rows whose condition is true, so unknown results from NULL comparisons do not pass its filter.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can combine two tables with LEFT OUTER JOIN, keeping all left-table rows even without a match.

required_facts.statement: LEFT OUTER JOIN returns matching combinations and preserves each unmatched left-table row.
For an unmatched left row, columns from the right table are filled with NULL.
Write SELECT a.column_name, b.column_name FROM table_a AS a LEFT OUTER JOIN table_b AS b ON a.key_column = b.key_column; with the table to preserve on the left.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can combine two tables with RIGHT OUTER JOIN, keeping all right-table rows even without a match.

required_facts.statement: RIGHT OUTER JOIN returns matching combinations and preserves each unmatched right-table row.
For an unmatched right row, columns from the left table are filled with NULL.
Write SELECT a.column_name, b.column_name FROM table_a AS a RIGHT OUTER JOIN table_b AS b ON a.key_column = b.key_column; with the table to preserve on the right.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can combine two tables with FULL OUTER JOIN, keeping unmatched rows from both sides.

required_facts.statement: FULL OUTER JOIN returns matching combinations and preserves unmatched rows from both tables.
Columns on the missing side of an unmatched row are filled with NULL.
Write SELECT a.column_name, b.column_name FROM table_a AS a FULL OUTER JOIN table_b AS b ON a.key_column = b.key_column; to preserve unmatched rows on either side.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can sort query results using ORDER BY, ascending or descending, on one or more columns.

required_facts.statement: Without ORDER BY, a query’s output order is unspecified.
ORDER BY column ASC sorts ascending and ORDER BY column DESC sorts descending; ASC is the default.
Write ORDER BY first_column ASC, second_column DESC to sort by the first column and break its ties with the second.
When not otherwise specified, NULL values sort last for ASC and first for DESC; NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST overrides that placement.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can write SQL queries following common business-reporting patterns (e.g. period-over-period, top-N, running totals) to answer reporting questions.

required_facts.statement: For a top-N report, compute the metric per group, order it descending, and limit the output: SELECT group_column, SUM(value_column) AS total FROM table_name GROUP BY group_column ORDER BY total DESC, group_column LIMIT n;
source_refs: postgres_docs#https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/queries-table-expressions.html — 7.2.3 — The GROUP BY and HAVING Clauses

required_facts.statement: A predictable limited result requires an ordering that determines which rows come first.
LAG(metric) OVER (ORDER BY period_column) retrieves the previous row’s metric for an ordered period comparison; the first row has NULL by default.
SUM(metric) OVER (ORDER BY period_column ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) computes an ordered running total over the rows through the current row.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can import and transform data into Power BI using Power Query (Get Data, shape, clean).

required_facts.statement: In Power BI Desktop, Home > Get data selects a connector and connects to a data source.
Choose Transform Data to open Power Query Editor and shape the data before loading it.
Change a column’s data type and remove unnecessary columns using the editor’s column commands; the transformations are recorded as applied steps.
Use Close & Apply to apply the transformations and load the shaped data.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can connect Tableau to a data source and prepare it (joins, extracts) for use in dashboards.

required_facts.statement: Select a connector in Tableau’s Connect pane and provide the source-specific connection information.
To create a physical join, drag the first table to the canvas, double-click it, then drag another table into that join canvas.
Select the join type and matching fields in the join dialog; inner keeps matches, left or right preserves its named side, and full outer preserves both sides.
An extract is a saved snapshot of data for analysis; select Extract on the Data Source page and configure the extract before saving it.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can assess an organization's current business capability/state as a baseline before proposing change.

required_facts.statement: A current-state assessment describes the present situation as a baseline for identifying improvements.
Record detailed notes about the current business situation in a structured current-state column.
Organize the current-state notes by the business areas being assessed so they can be compared with goals and gaps.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/gap-analysis — Categorize information and start your analysis; Assess current state

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can define a future-state vision describing the desired target state an initiative should achieve.

required_facts.statement: A desired-state definition states the objectives and situation the business wants to achieve.
Express the goal using a business outcome and measurable success target.
Write the desired objectives alongside the corresponding business areas in the desired-state column.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can identify the gap between current state and future state and articulate what must change to close it.

required_facts.statement: A gap is a specific difference between the current situation and the desired state.
Compare the current-state description with the desired-state objectives and list the specific differences keeping the business from those goals.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/gap-analysis — Assess current state; Define the desired state; Identify gaps

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can conduct a SWOT analysis identifying strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats for a business situation.

required_facts.statement: SWOT separates strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats in a business situation.
Strengths are internal advantages; weaknesses are internal limitations.
Opportunities are favorable external possibilities; threats are external factors that could harm success.
Create four labeled quadrants and place each factor according to whether it is internal or external and favorable or unfavorable.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/strategic-planning/swot-analysis — How to conduct a SWOT analysis

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can prioritize requirements using MoSCoW categories: Must, Should, Could, Won't have.

required_facts.statement: MoSCoW groups requirements as Must have, Should have, Could have, or Will not have for the scope being prioritized.
Must-have items are essential: without them the solution would not work or the project would be useless.
Should-have items are important but the solution can still work without them.
Could-have items are desirable but nonessential and have a smaller impact if omitted.
Will-not-have items are not needed within the prioritization scope and can be deprioritized or dropped.
Define the prioritization scope, discuss each item’s importance, and assign the category the group agrees fits it.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can classify features using the Kano model (basic, performance, delighter) to understand their effect on satisfaction.

required_facts.statement: Kano classifies features by how functionality relates to customer satisfaction.
Must-be or basic features are expected; their absence causes dissatisfaction, while their presence adds little satisfaction.
Performance features produce more satisfaction as their functionality improves.
Attractive or excitement features can delight users who did not expect them and may not notice their absence.
Use user evidence about satisfaction and the feature’s functionality to classify and discuss the appropriate category.
Indifferent features are those users feel neutral toward: changes in their functionality do not significantly increase or decrease customer satisfaction.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can build a weighted scoring model that ranks requirements/options by weighted criteria totals.

required_facts.statement: A weighted decision matrix compares options on criteria whose weights represent importance.
List the criteria and options, assign criterion weights, and score every option against each criterion using a consistent scale.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/decision-matrix — Define decision criteria; Assign weights; List the options; Score each option

required_facts.statement: Multiply each criterion score by its weight and add those products for the option’s total weighted score.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/decision-matrix — Calculate the weighted scores and make a decision

required_facts.statement: Compare the totals to rank the options; the highest total is typically the best choice under the chosen criteria and weights.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/decision-matrix — Calculate the weighted scores and make a decision

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can evaluate multiple candidate solutions/vendors against defined criteria and recommend the best fit.

required_facts.statement: Solution comparison uses defined decision criteria rather than an unstructured preference.
Score each candidate solution against the same criteria and multiply the scores by the corresponding importance weights.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/decision-matrix — Score each option; Calculate the weighted scores

required_facts.statement: Sum each candidate’s weighted scores, compare the totals, and explain the recommendation in terms of the criteria and scores.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/decision-matrix — Calculate the weighted scores and make a decision

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can develop a business case with cost-benefit analysis justifying a proposed initiative.

required_facts.statement: A business case justifies an initiative by describing the problem, possible solutions, expected benefits, and costs.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/business-case — What is a business case?; Key elements of a business case

required_facts.statement: List and estimate relevant costs and benefits over the period being evaluated, including direct and indirect effects.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/strategic-planning/cost-benefit-analysis — Key components of a cost-benefit analysis

required_facts.statement: Present the recommendation with the supporting financial assessment in the business case.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/business-case — Key elements of a business case

required_facts.statement: For a monetary-return estimate, calculate projected net return = total projected monetary benefits over the evaluation period − project cost, including the cost of the project itself rather than reporting gross savings alone.
source_refs: nngroup_articles#https://www.nngroup.com/articles/calculating-roi-design-projects/ — Step 3: Convert the UX Metric into the KPI; Step 4: Report Responsibly — Example: Health-Insurance Website

required_facts.statement: Interpret a positive projected monetary return as estimated benefits exceeding cost over that period, and report the assumptions and time horizon because the return is an estimate, not a promised financial outcome.
Calculate percentage ROI = (monetary benefits − costs) / costs × 100%, using net monetary return as the numerator and investment cost as the denominator.
source_refs: https://corporatefinanceinstitute.com/resources/accounting/return-on-investment-roi-formula/#ROI Formula; Is there an Excel formula for ROI?

required_facts.statement: Use the costs and monetary benefits for the stated evaluation period, include relevant costs rather than just a headline purchase cost, and use the same time period when comparing alternatives.
source_refs: https://corporatefinanceinstitute.com/resources/accounting/return-on-investment-roi-formula/#Limitations of the ROI Formula; Common Mistakes in Calculating ROI
atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/strategic-planning/cost-benefit-analysis — Key components of a cost-benefit analysis; Identify the costs and benefits

required_facts.statement: Net monetary return is the benefits-minus-costs amount in money, whereas percentage ROI expresses that net return relative to investment cost.
source_refs: https://corporatefinanceinstitute.com/resources/accounting/return-on-investment-roi-formula/#ROI Formula; What is the ROI percentage?

optional_enrichment.statement: Calculate net present value as the present value of future benefits minus the present value of future costs, using a consistent discount rate and evaluation period.
A positive net present value supports accepting the initiative on this financial criterion; a negative value argues against it, and zero indicates neither gain nor loss.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can apply multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) to compare options against several non-comparable dimensions systematically.

required_facts.statement: A decision matrix enables comparison across several criteria using explicit importance weights and scores.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/decision-matrix — What is a decision matrix template?

required_facts.statement: Define criteria and importance weights, then map each criterion’s performance values to a common rating scale with criterion-specific scoring definitions applied consistently to all options and higher ratings meaning better performance.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/decision-matrix — What is a decision matrix template?; Define decision criteria; Score each option against each criterion

required_facts.statement: Calculate each option’s total by multiplying its common-scale rating for each criterion by that criterion’s weight and summing these weighted ratings, rather than raw values in incompatible units, then compare totals for a defensible ranking.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/decision-matrix — Calculate the weighted scores and make a decision

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can compute and choose among mean, median, and mode to describe a dataset's central tendency.

required_facts.statement: The sample mean is computed as the sum of the observed values divided by the number of observations.
The median is the middle value when the data are ordered from smallest to largest; if there is an even number of observations, the median is the average of the two middle values.
The mode is the value that occurs most often in the data; there can be more than one mode.

The mean is more strongly affected by extreme observations (such as those in the tail of a skewed distribution) than the median, which is more robust to them; for this reason the median can better represent a typical value in a skewed dataset.

optional_enrichment.statement: A mode is a prominent peak in a distribution: a value or narrow range of values where observations are noticeably more concentrated than in neighboring regions.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can compute and interpret range, variance, and standard deviation to describe a dataset's spread.

required_facts.statement: The range of a data set is the largest value minus the smallest value.

The variance is computed by taking each observation's deviation from the mean, squaring it, summing the squared deviations, and dividing by n - 1 (one less than the number of observations); it is roughly the average squared distance of the observations from the mean.
The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, and it describes the typical distance of an observation from the mean.

The standard deviation is expressed in the same units as the original data, while the variance is expressed in squared units; the range is based only on the two most extreme values and ignores how the rest of the data are spread.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can write and refine user stories following INVEST criteria, including splitting oversized stories.

required_facts.statement: A user story states a persona’s need and its purpose using “As a [persona], I [want to], [so that].”
Refine oversized backlog items by breaking them into smaller, more precise items with clearer descriptions.
Split larger stories into smaller stories that can be completed within an iteration.
Use INVEST as a quality checklist for each rewritten or split story; if a criterion fails, consider rewording or rewriting the story.
Independent means stories should not overlap in concept and should be schedulable and implementable in any order; check whether a story can be implemented without requiring another story first.
Negotiable means a story captures the essential need rather than a fixed contract of feature details; check that details can be worked out collaboratively with the customer.
Valuable means a story delivers value to the customer; check that each split story describes a customer-valued result rather than only a technical layer.
Estimable means the team can approximate the work well enough to rank and schedule it; check that the team understands the story and its scope well enough to make an estimate.
Small means a story fits within an iteration; check the size of each proposed story and split work that cannot fit.
Testable means the desired result is clear enough to write a test for it; check that the customer can describe how to verify the story, and clarify stories whose result cannot be tested.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can maintain and groom a product backlog: ordering, refining, and keeping items ready for upcoming sprints.

required_facts.statement: A product backlog is an emergent, ordered list of work needed to improve the product.
Refinement breaks items into smaller, more precise items and adds details such as description, order, and size.
Review unclear or oversized items, clarify their details, split them as needed, and keep the backlog ordered.
Items that can be completed within one iteration are ready for selection; refinement usually provides the needed transparency.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can sequence prioritized requirements into delivery phases/releases based on priority, dependency, and capacity.

required_facts.statement: A roadmap sequences planned work against goals rather than listing disconnected features.
Group planned initiatives into a sequence such as Now, Next, and Later, linking the sequence to goals and tracking dependencies.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/roadmaps — Who is responsible for the product roadmap?; roadmap examples; Tips and tricks

required_facts.statement: Review the sequence as priorities and information change rather than treating the initial roadmap as fixed.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can collaboratively define testable acceptance criteria for a backlog item during refinement, establishing what 'done' means.

required_facts.statement: Acceptance criteria state the conditions used to determine whether a particular user story is satisfied.
Discuss what completing the story means, make the acceptance conditions testable, and document that shared understanding.
source_refs: atlassian_user_stories#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/user-stories — How to write user stories — Definition of done; What is in a user story?

required_facts.statement: Refinement adds detail to make backlog items more precise and understandable.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can write a clear business report/executive summary that communicates analysis findings to a business audience.

required_facts.statement: A report should be structured for its readers rather than assuming the findings speak for themselves.
source_refs: nngroup_articles#https://www.nngroup.com/articles/engaging-reports-presentations/ — Introduction; Structure Your Report for 3 Audiences

required_facts.statement: Put the key message in headlines for readers who only scan, then provide highlights and supporting detail for readers who need more.
Write at the level of detail the audience needs and select information that serves the report’s purpose.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can adapt the same technical content for both technical and non-technical audiences without changing its meaning.

required_facts.statement: The audience determines appropriate detail, terminology, and how information is communicated.
Use the audience’s language and explain an unfamiliar concept with a familiar analogy when useful.
Make the main ideas clear in headlines while preserving supporting detail for readers who need it.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can design and deliver a stakeholder presentation/slide deck communicating analysis or recommendations.

required_facts.statement: A presentation needs a narrative that makes findings meaningful to its audience rather than a bare list of data.
Structure the presentation around clear headlines, highlights, and supporting detail appropriate to different reader needs.
Use audience-appropriate language and connect findings to the recommendation being communicated.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can run a requirements walkthrough/demo session to review requirements and obtain sign-off from stakeholders.

required_facts.statement: Requirements review gives stakeholders and approvers the opportunity to confirm priorities and agree what will be delivered.
Plan a review around the documented goal, scope, requirements, assumptions, and open questions.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Step 4: Document requirements in one shared place

required_facts.statement: Record decisions in the shared requirements document so agreement and unresolved questions remain visible.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Step 4: Document requirements in one shared place

required_facts.statement: Close the walkthrough agenda by asking designated approvers to approve the reviewed requirements or state outstanding conditions, and record the approval outcome, approvers, and any unresolved conditions in the shared decision log.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Step 2: Identify stakeholders and decision-makers; Step 5: Prioritize and validate requirements; What to include in a requirements document — Open questions, Decision log

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can draw a scope/context diagram showing a system's boundary and its external actors/interfaces.

required_facts.statement: A context diagram represents the system as a single element with a boundary separating it from external entities.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/context-diagram — What is a system context diagram?

required_facts.statement: Define the system’s purpose and boundary and identify its external actors and connected systems.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/context-diagram — How to create a system context diagram

required_facts.statement: Draw the system centrally, place external entities around it, and use labeled directional arrows to show exchanges.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/context-diagram — How to create a system context diagram

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can break down a business function into a hierarchy of sub-functions via functional decomposition.

required_facts.statement: Hierarchical decomposition represents a larger goal as major tasks and breaks those tasks into smaller parts.
Start with the top-level goal, draw its major parts below it, and break each part into relevant subparts.
Choose the number of decomposition levels according to the complexity and detail needed.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can use relative and absolute cell references and basic formulas (SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT) in a spreadsheet.

required_facts.statement: A spreadsheet formula starts with = and may combine cell references, operators, and functions.
source_refs: excel_support#https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/excel/get-started/overview-of-formulas-in-excel — The parts of an Excel formula

required_facts.statement: A relative reference such as A1 changes when the formula is copied to a different position.
An absolute reference such as $A$1 keeps its row and column fixed when copied; $A1 or A$1 fixes just one part.
Use =SUM(range) to total values, =AVERAGE(range) for their arithmetic mean, and =COUNT(range) to count numeric cells.
Copy a formula containing relative and fixed references and inspect how each reference changes according to the destination.
AVERAGE ignores empty cells and text in a referenced range but includes cells containing zero.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can build a pivot table to summarize and cross-tabulate raw spreadsheet data.

required_facts.statement: A PivotTable is a tool to calculate, summarize, and analyze data that lets you see comparisons, patterns, and trends in your data.
source_refs: excel_pivottable_guide#Create a PivotTable to analyze worksheet data

required_facts.statement: To create a PivotTable, select the data cells, select Insert > PivotTable, choose where to place the PivotTable report, and select OK.
source_refs: excel_pivottable_guide#Create a PivotTable in Excel for Windows

required_facts.statement: To add a field to the PivotTable, select its checkbox in the PivotTable Fields pane; selected fields are added to their default areas, with non-numeric fields added to Rows and numeric fields added to Values, and a field can be moved to a different area by dragging it there.

Filters area fields are shown as top-level report filters above the PivotTable; Columns area fields are shown as Column Labels at the top of the PivotTable; Rows area fields are shown as Row Labels on the left side of the PivotTable; Values area fields are shown as summarized numeric values in the PivotTable.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can use lookup functions (VLOOKUP/XLOOKUP/INDEX-MATCH) to retrieve a value from another table based on a key match.

required_facts.statement: A lookup retrieves a value associated with a matching key.
Use =XLOOKUP(key, lookup_range, return_range) to find a key and return the corresponding value; exact match is the default.
Use =VLOOKUP(key, table_range, column_number, FALSE) for an exact match in the first column and a return value from the specified column to its right.
If VLOOKUP’s final argument is omitted or TRUE, it uses approximate matching and expects the first column sorted.
Use =INDEX(return_range, MATCH(key, lookup_range, 0)) to return the value at the exact key’s position.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can write conditional formulas (IF, nested IF, IFS) that return different results based on a condition.

required_facts.statement: IF(logical_test, value_if_true, value_if_false) returns one of two results according to the test.
Use =IF(test1, result1, IF(test2, result2, result3)) to express three ordered alternatives.
source_refs: excel_support#https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/excel/functions/if-function — Simple IF examples — discussion of nesting multiple comparisons

required_facts.statement: IFS(test1, result1, test2, result2, ...) returns the result for the first true condition.
A final TRUE condition in IFS supplies a default result; without a true condition, IFS returns #N/A.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can build a chart in a spreadsheet that correctly visualizes a given dataset and question.

required_facts.statement: Choose the visualization according to the question: bars compare categories and lines show trends over time.
source_refs: powerbi_docs#https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-bi/visuals/power-bi-visualization-types-for-reports-and-q-and-a — Charts for comparison and trends — Bar and column charts; Line charts

required_facts.statement: Give the chart a clear title and labels so readers can interpret the intended comparison.
source_refs: powerbi_docs#https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-bi/create-reports/service-dashboards-design-tips — Consider your audience; Tell a story on one screen

required_facts.statement: In Excel for the web, select the worksheet range containing the data, then use Insert > Charts to choose a suitable chart type.

Right-click the chart and choose Select Data; in Data > Setup assign the category-cell range to Horizontal Axis > Horizontal Field and add the value-cell range under Vertical Axis > Add Field, checking that the fields occupy the intended axes.
source_refs: excel_support#https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/excel/get-started/create-a-chart-from-start-to-finish — 2. Edit the Data — Add, remove or modify a data series; Swap vertical and horizontal axis

required_facts.statement: Check the source range and plotted series in the chart task pane, correcting series names or ranges as needed, then use Format to check the chart title, axis titles, and displayed data labels.
source_refs: excel_support#https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/excel/get-started/create-a-chart-from-start-to-finish — 2. Edit the Data; 3. Customize your chart — Add, remove or modify the title; Add, remove or modify the titles of your axis; Add, remove or modify data labels

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can produce a quick, one-off business analysis report in a spreadsheet in response to an ad hoc stakeholder request.

required_facts.statement: Start by clarifying the business outcome or question the analysis should address.
A spreadsheet pivot table can summarize source data with fields placed in Rows, Columns, and Values.
source_refs: excel_support#https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/create-a-pivottable-to-analyze-worksheet-data-a9a84538-bfe9-40a9-a8e9-f99134456576 — Working with the PivotTable Fields pane

required_facts.statement: Present the answer prominently and include enough supporting detail for the audience to understand it.
Select a table or range, insert a PivotTable, place grouping fields in Rows and the metric in Values, and select an aggregation that answers the business question.
source_refs: excel_support#https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/create-a-pivottable-to-analyze-worksheet-data-a9a84538-bfe9-40a9-a8e9-f99134456576 — Insert a PivotTable; Working with PivotTable Values

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can participate in sprint planning as a BA: clarifying requirements and acceptance criteria so the team can commit to a sprint's scope.

required_facts.statement: Sprint Planning collaboratively establishes the work for the iteration.
Review important backlog items collaboratively and select work that can be completed within the iteration.
Inspect candidate items for clear descriptions and sufficient detail, and refine uncertain items before selection.
Selection considers the Developers’ capacity and past performance rather than an externally imposed commitment.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can collaborate effectively as a BA with the Product Owner and delivery team across the sprint cycle.

required_facts.statement: The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing product value and effective backlog management.
The Product Owner may delegate backlog-management work but remains accountable for it.
Developers are responsible for sizing the work and deciding how selected work is performed.
Clarify backlog items collaboratively while respecting the Product Owner’s ordering accountability and the Developers’ delivery decisions.
source_refs: scrum_guide#https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html — Product Owner; Product Backlog; Sprint Planning

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can participate in the daily standup as a BA, surfacing blockers relevant to requirements/clarification without turning it into a status meeting.

required_facts.statement: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for Developers focused on progress toward the Sprint Goal and an actionable plan.
Participation by other Scrum accountabilities as Developers depends on actively working on iteration backlog items.
Give an update that identifies an impediment or needed coordination affecting the goal and the next work plan.
Move detailed replanning discussion outside the Daily Scrum rather than extending the event.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can participate in sprint review as a BA, helping validate delivered work against acceptance criteria with stakeholders.

required_facts.statement: The Sprint Review inspects the outcome with stakeholders and determines future adaptations; it is a working session rather than just a presentation.
Acceptance criteria provide the story-specific conditions used to judge whether delivered behavior satisfies the need.
Compare the demonstrated behavior with those conditions and discuss differences with the stakeholders.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can participate in a sprint retrospective as a BA, contributing to identifying process improvements for the team.

required_facts.statement: The Sprint Retrospective plans ways to improve quality and effectiveness.
Review what went well, what problems occurred, and how they were or were not solved, considering interactions, processes, and tools.
Identify a concrete change that would improve effectiveness and arrange to address the most helpful improvements promptly.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can apply the Five Whys technique to trace a problem back to its root cause by repeatedly asking why.

required_facts.statement: Five Whys traces a problem’s cause by repeatedly asking why the previous explanation occurred.
Write the problem, ask why it happened, record the answer, and ask why that answer happened to extend the causal chain.
Five is a guide rather than a required stopping point; use the chain to reach an underlying cause rather than restating the symptom.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can build a fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram organizing candidate causes of a problem into standard categories.

required_facts.statement: A fishbone diagram organizes possible causes of a problem to support root cause analysis.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/fishbone-diagram — What is a fishbone diagram template?

required_facts.statement: Write a specific problem statement, select cause categories appropriate to the problem, and brainstorm potential causes with the team.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/fishbone-diagram — Define the problem; Choose categories; Brainstorm potential causes

required_facts.statement: Place each proposed cause under its category branch to expose patterns; then analyze the proposed causes and agree actions addressing the root cause.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/fishbone-diagram — Organize causes; Analyze the diagram; Develop an action plan

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can define and apply a Definition of Done (DoD) as the team-wide quality bar every backlog item must meet before being called complete.

required_facts.statement: The Definition of Done describes the state of an increment when it meets the required quality measures.
The Scrum Team follows a shared Definition of Done, at least as rigorous as any organizational standard.
An item that does not meet the Definition of Done cannot be released or presented at the Sprint Review.
Check the completed work against the defined quality criteria and identify any unmet criterion before calling it done.
Story acceptance criteria specify completion conditions for that particular story rather than replacing the shared quality standard.

briefs.learning_objective: Learner can design a star schema (fact and dimension tables) for a BI data model to support efficient analytical queries.

required_facts.statement: A star schema separates tables describing business entities from tables storing observations or events.
Dimension tables describe entities and their attributes; their key columns identify rows.
Fact tables store observations or events with dimension keys and often numeric measures.
Choose the fact table’s grain so its rows describe a consistent level of detail.
